content.title: La misma hora, distinto destino
content.story:
Clara sostenía los dos cafés mientras Mateo buscaba los billetes en el teléfono. En el andén, bajo un reloj que parecía adelantarse por pura mala intención, los viajeros se agrupaban junto a las marcas de sus respectivos vagones.

—Coche cuatro —dijo Mateo—. Nos queda cerca.

Clara le tendió un café y sacó su billete impreso. Lo había doblado con tanto cuidado que tuvo que alisarlo sobre la maleta para leerlo.

—Yo voy en el siete.

—Bueno, nos cambiamos cuando subamos.

Ella no contestó. Miró la pantalla del teléfono de Mateo y después volvió a mirar el papel.

—¿Por qué el tuyo dice Valladolid?

Mateo acercó el teléfono, como si la distancia pudiera haber alterado las letras.

—Porque vamos a Valladolid.

—Vamos a Salamanca.

Durante unos segundos, ninguno dijo nada. El desconcierto de Mateo se manifestó en un gesto pequeño: levantó la tapa del café, comprobó algo que no necesitaba comprobar y volvió a cerrarla.

—Tú dijiste que querías volver allí —respondió al fin.

—A Salamanca. Donde estudiamos.

—Estudiamos en las dos ciudades.

—Pero cuando te dije «volvamos», estábamos viendo las fotos del piso de Salamanca.

Mateo deslizó el dedo por la pantalla. Había comprado su billete la noche de aquella conversación, antes de que Clara le enviara el suyo. Cuando recibió el mensaje, solo había comprobado la hora de salida.

—Diez y veinte —murmuró—. Coincidía.

—La hora, sí.

La precisión de Clara le molestó más que un reproche abierto. Ella lo notó y bajó la vista al papel. Tampoco había mirado el billete de Mateo; había dado por sentado que ambos recordaban la misma ciudad cuando hablaban de regresar.

Por los altavoces anunciaron el tren a Valladolid. Un hombre que estaba a su lado levantó la maleta y echó a andar. Mateo no se movió.

—Si hubiéramos comprobado los destinos ayer, habríamos podido cambiar uno de los billetes —dijo Clara.

—Si hubieras dicho Salamanca…

Se interrumpió. Clara arqueó una ceja, pero no aprovechó la ocasión.

—Si tú hubieras preguntado, también —añadió, sin dureza.

Mateo soltó una risa breve.

—Qué bien nos repartimos la culpa cuando ya no sirve de nada.

Clara bebió un sorbo. El café estaba demasiado caliente; agradeció tener una razón para no responder enseguida. A su alrededor, el andén empezaba a vaciarse.

—¿Querías ir a Valladolid? —preguntó.

—Pensaba que tú querías.

—Eso no es lo que te he preguntado.

Mateo miró hacia la puerta del coche cuatro. En Valladolid seguía viviendo su hermano, con quien llevaba meses intercambiando mensajes que ninguno terminaba de contestar.

—No me habría disgustado —admitió.

Clara asintió despacio. El equívoco ya no consistía únicamente en haber entendido mal un nombre: cada uno había imaginado un viaje que el otro, al parecer, debía desear también.

—Podemos ir por separado —dijo ella—. No sería una tragedia.

—No.

Pero Mateo lo dijo a regañadientes, con la misma resistencia con que habría aceptado quedarse fuera de una fotografía.

Clara guardó su billete. Su tren salía de otro andén; todavía tenía unos minutos para llegar. Tiró del asa de la maleta y luego la soltó.

—Voy a preguntar si puedo cambiarlo por uno a Valladolid.

—¿Y Salamanca?

—Seguirá allí. Pero la próxima vez elegimos la ciudad antes de comprar nada.

Mateo tomó la maleta de Clara sin preguntarle. Ella se la dejó llevar.

Caminaron hacia las escaleras, en dirección contraria a los últimos pasajeros. Al llegar al primer peldaño, Mateo sacó de nuevo el teléfono.

—También puedo cambiar el mío —dijo.

Clara lo miró. Esta vez, antes de seguir andando, se detuvieron a decidir qué querían los dos.

glossary.meaning: To hold or support something. “Sostenía” is imperfect, describing an action in progress in the background.
Coffee; here also a serving or cup of coffee.
While; links two actions happening at the same time.
To look for. The imperfect describes Mateo's ongoing search.
A train ticket.
A phone, used here to display a digital ticket.
A railway platform.
Under or beneath something.
A clock.
To seem or appear.
For a clock to run ahead; here the clock seems to hurry deliberately.
Out of sheer malice; humorously attributes a spiteful motive to the clock.
A traveler.
To gather in groups. The imperfect describes the scene around the friends.
Beside or next to.
A marking indicating where passengers should wait.
Corresponding to each person or group: each traveler's own carriage.
A railway carriage.
A railway carriage, identified here by its number.
To say. “Dijo” and “dijiste” report completed past speech; “dice” is present, referring to what the ticket shows.
To be nearby; “nos” indicates that the carriage is close to where they are.
To hand or hold something out to someone.
To take something out.
Printed, rather than displayed digitally; masculine singular to agree with “billete.”
To fold. “Había doblado” describes an action completed before the scene's main past events.
So carefully that; introduces the consequence of the care taken.
To have to do something. “Tuvo que” expresses a necessity on that past occasion.
To smooth or flatten something. In “alisarlo,” “lo” refers to the folded ticket.
On top of; the suitcase provides a surface for the ticket.
A suitcase.
To read. The attached “lo” refers to the ticket.
To go or travel. “Voy” and “vamos” are present forms; “voy en el siete” identifies Clara's assigned carriage.
To move to another carriage or seat. The present form here expresses their proposed future arrangement.
When; “cuando subamos” uses the subjunctive because boarding is still in the future.
To board the train. “Subamos” is present subjunctive after “cuando” for an anticipated event.
To answer or reply, whether in conversation or to a message.
To look at.
A screen.
Afterward or then.
To do something again, rather than return to a place.
Paper; here the printed ticket.
Why; written as two words with an accent in a question.
Yours; “el tuyo” replaces “your ticket.”
To bring something closer.
As if; introduces an imagined comparison and takes a past subjunctive form here.
Distance; here the distance between Mateo and the phone screen.
To be able to or have the possibility of doing something. “Pudiera” is subjunctive; “puedo” and “podemos” are present.
To change or modify; humorously used of the destination's written letters.
A letter of the alphabet.
Because; gives a reason, unlike interrogative “por qué.”
For or during a period of time.
A second, a short unit of time.
Neither one of the two friends. It takes a singular verb here.
Nothing or anything. With “no” or “ninguno,” it forms a normal Spanish negative construction.
Bewilderment caused by the unexpected ticket mismatch.
To reveal or show itself; Mateo's confusion becomes visible in his gesture.
A gesture or small physical action expressing a feeling.
Small or slight.
To lift something.
A lid, here on a coffee cup.
To check or verify. “Había comprobado” refers to an earlier check; “hubiéramos comprobado” imagines a check that did not happen.
Something, left unspecified.
To need to do something.
To close. The attached “la” in “cerrarla” refers to the lid.
To want. The imperfect forms describe wishes or intentions in the past.
To return to a place. “Volvamos” is a subjunctive form used as a suggestion: let's go back.
There, referring to a previously mentioned place.
To answer or respond.
At last or finally, after a pause.
Where; introduces the place in which they studied.
To study. “Estudiamos” has the same form in the present and preterite; here it refers to their past studies.
A city.
But; marks a contrast or objection.
To be looking at something. The imperfect progressive describes what they were doing during the earlier conversation.
A photograph; a common short form of “fotografía.”
An apartment or flat, here their former accommodation in Salamanca.
To slide or move smoothly; here moving a finger across a touchscreen.
A finger.
To buy. “Había comprado” places the ticket purchase before the later discovery.
Night; here the evening or night of their earlier conversation.
That; a feminine demonstrative referring back to the earlier conversation.
A conversation.
Before; followed here by imperfect subjunctive “enviara” to place the sending after the purchase.
To send. “Enviara” is imperfect subjunctive after “antes de que.”
His or hers. “El suyo” refers here to Clara's ticket.
To receive.
A message, here sent by phone.
Only; he checked the departure time and nothing else.
A time shown on the clock or specified for departure.
Departure; “hora de salida” is the departure time.
Ten twenty, the departure time.
To murmur or speak quietly.
To match or be the same; the tickets' departure times matched.
Exactness or precision, here Clara's pointed correction about what matched.
To bother or irritate. “Le” identifies Mateo as the person affected.
More than; compares how irritating Clara's precision was with an explicit reproach.
A reproach: an expression of blame or disapproval.
Open or explicit, rather than merely implied.
To notice or detect.
To lower one's gaze or look down.
Not either; adds another negative fact.
To take something for granted without checking. “Había dado” shows that this assumption preceded the discovery.
Both, referring to the two friends.
To remember or have something in mind.
The same; its ending agrees with the noun it describes.
To talk about something.
To return, here to a city connected with their shared past.
A loudspeaker used for station announcements.
To announce. The third-person plural leaves the announcers unspecified.
A train.
A man.
Beside him or them.
To start walking; “echar a” emphasizes the start of an action.
To move or change position.
If; introduces a condition. Past subjunctive with conditional perfect describes an unreal past alternative.
To have checked. “Hubiéramos comprobado” is pluperfect subjunctive: if we had checked, although they did not.
A destination, the place a train or traveler is going.
Yesterday.
To have been able to. “Habríamos podido” is conditional perfect, expressing an unreal past opportunity.
To change or exchange a ticket. Attached pronouns in “cambiarlo” and “cambiarle” are not interchangeable; only “cambiarlo” occurs here and refers to the ticket.
To have said. “Hubieras dicho” imagines Mateo having been explicitly told the destination.
To break off one's own speech.
To raise an eyebrow, expressing doubt, challenge, or disbelief.
To make use of or seize an opportunity; here an opportunity to press the blame.
An opportunity or opening.
To have asked. “Hubieras preguntado” imagines an earlier question that Mateo did not ask.
Also or too; adds another possibility or responsibility.
To add something to what has already been said.
Without harshness; describes a gentle rather than cutting tone.
To let out a laugh.
Brief or short-lasting.
How well; used ironically here to mock how efficiently they distribute blame.
To divide or share something between themselves, here responsibility for the mistake.
Blame or responsibility for something going wrong.
Now or already; here signals that the useful moment for assigning blame has passed.
To be of no use or serve no purpose.
To drink.
A sip, a small amount drunk at once.
Too or excessively; here the coffee is hotter than comfortable.
Hot.
To be grateful for or welcome something; here Clara welcomes an excuse to delay answering.
To have. “Tenía” is imperfect, describing the time she still had available.
A reason or explanation, here for not answering immediately.
Immediately or right away.
Around him or her; here around Clara.
To begin to do something. The imperfect shows the process starting in the background.
To empty out; here the platform gradually loses its passengers.
To ask a question. “Preguntarle” attaches the pronoun meaning 'to her' in this context.
To think or believe. The imperfect presents Mateo's previous assumption.
That is not what; rejects an answer as not addressing the actual question.
To have asked. “He preguntado” is present perfect, referring to Clara's immediately preceding question.
Toward, indicating the direction of a look or movement.
A door, here the entrance to the carriage.
To still be living somewhere; “seguía” indicates continuation from an earlier time.
A brother.
With whom; refers back to Mateo's brother.
To have been doing something for months. Followed by a gerund, it expresses elapsed duration.
To exchange, here messages sent back and forth.
To finish doing something. Here neither brother fully answers the messages.
I wouldn't have minded; an understated admission that he would have welcomed the visit. Conditional perfect.
To admit or acknowledge something previously left unsaid.
To nod in agreement or acknowledgment.
Slowly.
A misunderstanding based on an ambiguous or mistaken interpretation.
To consist in or be a matter of; identifies what the misunderstanding really involved.
Only or solely.
To misunderstand or interpret incorrectly.
A name, here the name of a destination.
Each one, considered individually.
To imagine or mentally picture.
A trip or journey.
The other person; each friend's companion.
Apparently or seemingly; marks an inference rather than certainty.
To be supposed or expected to; here each assumed the other ought to want the same trip.
To desire or want.
Separately, rather than traveling together.
To be. “Sería” is conditional, presenting separate travel as a hypothetical possibility.
A tragedy or disaster; used figuratively for a disappointing but manageable situation.
Reluctantly, with noticeable unwillingness.
Resistance or unwillingness to accept something.
To accept. “Habría aceptado” is conditional perfect, describing an imagined reaction.
To remain outside or be left out of something; here exclusion from a shared photograph.
A photograph.
To put something away.
To depart. “Salía” is imperfect, referring to the train's scheduled departure from another platform.
Another or different; here a platform different from Mateo's.
Still; indicates that some time remains.
A minute.
To arrive or reach a place.
To pull on something.
A handle, here on a suitcase. This feminine noun takes “el” in the singular because it begins with stressed a.
Then or afterward.
To release or let go of something, here the suitcase handle.
To be going to do something; expresses Clara's immediate intention.
To exchange something for something else, here one ticket for another.
To remain or continue. “Seguirá allí” means Salamanca will still be there in the future.
Next time.
To choose. “Elegimos” is present in form but here states their plan for next time.
Before; followed here by an infinitive rather than a conjugated clause.
To take or pick up, here taking charge of Clara's suitcase.
To let someone carry something. In “se la dejó llevar,” “la” refers to the suitcase and “se” to Mateo.
To walk.
Stairs or a staircase.
In the opposite direction to.
Last or remaining; here the final passengers leaving the platform.
A passenger.
On arriving or when they reached; “al” plus infinitive locates another action in time.
First; the shortened masculine form of “primero” before a singular noun.
An individual stair or step.
Again.
Mine; “el mío” replaces “my ticket.”
This time, contrasting with their earlier failure to discuss their wishes.
To continue walking; “seguir” plus a gerund expresses continuation.
To stop or pause. “Se detuvieron” is a completed past action.
To decide.
What; accented in an indirect question such as deciding what they wanted.
Both of them, emphasizing their shared wishes.

content.title: Dos maneras de irse
content.story:
A Clara le gustaba llegar a las estaciones con tiempo suficiente para tomar un café; a Julián, con el justo para no tener que esperar. Aquella mañana habían llegado a un término medio: el café quemaba todavía y el tren de Clara salía en doce minutos.

—Andén cuatro —dijo ella, mirando la pantalla—. Vamos.

Julián sostuvo su billete junto al de Clara, como quien comprueba una dirección antes de echar una carta al buzón. Luego apartó el vaso de la boca.

—El mío dice andén siete.

—Habrá cambiado.

—También dice Salamanca.

Clara bajó la vista. En su billete figuraba Valladolid, con una claridad que de pronto le pareció insolente.

Durante unos segundos ninguno habló. A su alrededor, las ruedas de las maletas seguían golpeando las juntas del suelo; una familia discutía dónde había guardado los bocadillos. El desconcierto de los dos no alteraba en absoluto el funcionamiento de la estación.

—Tú vas a Salamanca —dijo Clara—. Yo voy a Valladolid.

—Eso parece.

No sonrió. Ella agradeció que no intentara convertirlo inmediatamente en una anécdota.

Habían organizado la escapada por mensajes, entre reuniones y cenas tardías. Clara había propuesto Valladolid el lunes. El martes, Julián había enviado la fotografía de un patio en Salamanca y había escrito: «Aquí podríamos pasar el sábado». Ella había respondido: «Perfecto. Me encargo de lo mío».

—Con “perfecto” quería decir que el patio era precioso —explicó Clara.

—Yo entendí que cambiábamos de plan.

—¿Sin decirlo?

La pregunta salió más afilada de lo que pretendía. Julián dobló ligeramente el billete y volvió a alisarlo.

—Tú tampoco dijiste que seguíamos con el anterior.

Clara estuvo a punto de responder que no era lo mismo. Pero recordó que, al comprar su pasaje, había dado por sentado que Julián compraría otro idéntico. Ni siquiera le había enviado una captura.

—Si hubiéramos comparado los billetes anoche, nos habríamos ahorrado esto —dijo.

—Anoche me mandaste una foto de tu maleta.

—Y tú dijiste que llevaba demasiados zapatos.

—Los llevas.

Esta vez sí sonrieron, aunque el reproche seguía allí, menos dirigido al otro que a la facilidad con que cada uno había confundido su propia certeza con un acuerdo.

Por los altavoces anunciaron el embarque para Valladolid. Clara miró hacia las escaleras del andén cuatro. Había elegido un restaurante, consultado el tiempo y reservado una habitación con dos camas. Todo aquel pequeño futuro seguía esperándola, pero ahora le resultaba extraño entrar en él sola.

—Podemos preguntar si te cambian el billete —propuso.

Julián señaló la fila de atención al cliente. Apenas avanzaba.

—Y perder tu tren mientras intentamos salvar el mío.

—O ir a Salamanca.

Él la miró con una atención que la hizo dejar de buscar argumentos.

—¿Quieres ir a Salamanca o quieres zanjar esto cuanto antes?

Clara apoyó el café en una repisa. Para resolver el equívoco bastaba con elegir una ciudad; para que ninguno sintiera que había cedido por cansancio, hacía falta algo más.

—Quiero que pasemos el sábado juntos. Lo de la ciudad me importa menos. Pero no quiero decidir mientras corremos.

Julián asintió y dejó su vaso junto al de ella.

—Entonces no corremos.

Se apartaron del paso de los viajeros. Clara abrió en el teléfono la reserva del hotel; Julián buscó las condiciones de su billete. Perderían dinero, seguramente, y tendrían que reorganizar la mañana. Ninguno fingió que aquello daba igual.

—Primero averiguamos qué podemos cambiar —dijo ella—. Después elegimos.

—Y esta vez lo decimos con todas las letras.

Clara le mostró la pantalla antes de pulsar nada. Al fondo, seguían llamando a los pasajeros de su tren.

A misunderstanding arising from ambiguity or a mistaken interpretation.
An expression or feeling of blame or disappointment.
To settle or put an end to an issue or disagreement.

glossary.meaning: To be about to do something; here, Clara nearly replies but stops herself.
To give in or yield; here, to accept the other's choice reluctantly.
Explicitly and unambiguously, leaving nothing merely implied.
